= Create and compile a CAL project from the scratch = You have now the basic knowledge to create your own CAL project from the scratch. In the following you will find the steps to follow and the main points to be aware of: * create a directory for your project and copy into it the <tt>crt0ram.S</tt>, <tt>makefile</tt> <tt>conf.oil</tt> files. The latter will be opportunely modified in a secon moment. * create in the project's directory your <tt>main.c</tt> file and insert here your code * create CAL actors and/or system actors and a netlist file combining all the actors together. = Create your first project: cal_demo =
We are now ready to create our first project and compile it. This first demo, called cal_demo, is composed of two system actors, a switch actor and a led actor called <tt>art_switch.c</tt> and <tt>art_led.c</tt>. These files are created in C language and can be found, along with the appropriate CAL files, into Erika's repository in: <tt>~/Evidence/Erika/ee/contrib/cal/src</tt>. The two system actors are combined in a netlist file named <tt>switchled.nl</tt> that you can find into cal_demo's directory. The purpose of this demo is to read the state of the switches and button residing on the FPG-EYE and produce it switching on/off the appropriate leds on the board itself.
Open the Lattice Mico32 System and press the C/C++ button on the status bar: [[File:eclipse_empty_screen.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the C/C++ button that must be pressed]]
Let's create a standard C project: [[File:eclipse-standard-make-project.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the button which must be pressed to create a standard C project]]
Give the project a name you like (i.e. cal_demo) and beware not to use the default location suggested by the program but the directory where resides the cal_demo into the Erika's trunk: [[File:cal-demo-project-settings.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows how to properly edit the project settings for the cal_demo project]] Press the Finish button and your project will be added to the list of C/C++ projects.
Here's how your newly created project appears: [[File:cal_demo_project_created.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the files you will find once created a new cal_demo project]] The files present at this stage of the project are: * main.c: main file project needed to initialize components of the FPG-EYE that will be used in the project. The user can place here it's own code. * switchled.nl: the netlist file listing the actors present in our CAL project; it's because of netlist files that actors will be automatically included in the building process. To better understand where the system actors were injected into ERIKA's repository and where newly created CAL actors have to be saved have a look [[CAL support on ERIKA Enterprise | here]] * conf.oil: configuration file, part of the OSEK/VDX standard, that is used for OS and application configuration. You will find here, as application sources, both main.c and switchled.nl files. For further explanation about oil files please have a look at [[Tutorial: RT-Druid and OIL basics | this tutorial]] * makefile: makefile of our project * crt0ram.S: file that implements boot-code and exception handlers
To build the project right click on the cal_demo project and press the Build Project button: [[File:cal_demo_build_project.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows how to build the cal_demo project]]
The result of the compilation is shown in the next screenshot: [[File:cal_demo_compilation_successful.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the results of a correct building process]] As you can see in the previous screenshot there's a newly created folder named <tt>output/folder</tt> where object and dependency files are placed. Here you can find: * <tt>switchled.depend</tt> and <tt>switchled.xdf</tt>: these files are automatically created by the ACTORS makefiles in the process of creating the <tt>switchled.c</tt> from the netlist file present in our project * out.elf: the executable file
To clean the project right click on the cal_demo project and press the Clean Project button: [[File:cal_demo_clean_project.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows how to clean a project]]
= Create your second project: cal_demo_cal_actors =
The main point of this second demo is that we used a CAL actor named <tt>gen.cal</tt>, a counter, instead of the previously used <tt>art_switch.c</tt> system actor; our counter is combined with the <tt>art_led.c</tt> system actor by the <tt>genled.nl</tt>. Both the netlist and the CAL actor files are placed in the project's directory. The purpose of this demo is to visualize the number produced by the counter switching on/off appropriately the leds placed into the FPG-EYE board
In order to create the project follow the steps described in the previous example, paying attention to the settings of the project:
[[File:cal_demo_cal_actors_project_settings.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows how to properly edit the project settings for the cal_demo_cal_actors project]]
Here's how your newly created project appears: [[File:cal_demo_cal_actors_project_created.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the files you will find once created a new cal_demo_cal_actors project]]
Looking at the files present at this stage and comparing them with the previous cal_demo example the main differences you will note are: * gen.cal: this is the CAL actor * genled.nl: this is the new netlist file. Please note the different nomenclature it to be used to address a system actor or a CAL one. To fully understand the meaning of the this nomenclature please refer to [[CAL support on ERIKA Enterprise | this tutorial]] * conf.oil: the application sources now present are main.c and genled.nl.
The result of a successful compilation (to be undertaken as explained in the previous example) is shown in the next screenshot: [[File:cal_demo_cal_actors_compilation_successful.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the results of a correct building process of the cal_demo_cal_actors project]]
Looking at the newly created files you will notice some differences comparing with the previous example: * <tt>output/obj</tt>: there is now <tt>gen_0.c</tt> which is the C file created from the <tt>gen.cal</tt> CAL actor. In the process of obtaing <tt>gen_0.c</tt> and <tt>genled.c</tt> files the ACTORS makefiles created also <tt>gen_0.xlim</tt>, <tt>gen_0.par</tt> and <tt>art_led_0.par</tt> files that are stored into the project's directory.
= Create and compile a CAL project from the scratch = You have now the basic knowledge to create your own CAL project from the scratch. In the following you will find the steps to follow and the main points to be aware of: * create a directory for your project and copy into it the <tt>crt0ram.S</tt>, <tt>makefile</tt> <tt>conf.oil</tt> files. The latter will be opportunely modified in a secon moment. * create in the project's directory your <tt>main.c</tt> file and insert here your code * create CAL actors and/or system actors and a netlist file combining all the actors together. Please note that: ** CAL actors are created in CAL language and have to be placed in the project's directory. ** system actors have to be written in C language and placed in <tt>contrib/cal/src</tt> directory as explained in [[CAL support on ERIKA Enterprise | this tutorial]]. * edit the <tt>conf.oil</tt> file in order to add as applications sources your main C file and your netlist. Moreover pay attention to link correctly your platform library according to where it is placed on your system. For further explanation about oil files please have a look at [[Tutorial: RT-Druid and OIL basics | this tutorial]]
Now build your CAL application following the previous examples.

Please note that: ** CAL actors are created in CAL language and have to be placed in the project's directory. ** system actors have to be written in C language and placed in <tt>contrib/cal/src</tt> directory as explained in [[CAL support on ERIKA Enterprise | this tutorial]]. * edit the <tt>conf.oil</tt> file in order to add as applications sources your main C file and your netlist. Moreover pay attention to link correctly your platform library according to where it is placed on your system. For further explanation about oil files please have a look at [[Tutorial: RT-Druid and OIL basics | this tutorial]]
Now build your CAL application following the previous examples.

== Introduction ==
This small tutorial describes the steps to follow in order to create and compile two demo applications with CAL actors in Erika Enterprise using a Lattice Mico32 platform.
For a brief introduction to CAL language and CAL actors please refer to [[Brief introduction to the CAL language]]
== Prerequisites ==
Make sure you have correctly installed both LatticeMico32 System and ispVM System on your Linux machine and exported all the environment variables needed for compiling a project. For any help please have a look at [[Tutorial: Installing CAL with ERIKA Enterprise]].
In order to compile a project it is essential to create a library for the Lattice Mico32 platform as explained in [[Tutorial: Mico32 library for ERIKA]].
== Create your first project: cal_demo ==
We are now ready to create our first project and compile it. This first demo, called cal_demo, is composed of two system actors, a switch actor and a led actor called <tt>art_switch.c</tt> and <tt>art_led.c</tt>. These files are created in C language and can be found, along with the appropriate CAL files, into Erika's repository in: <tt>~/Evidence/Erika/ee/contrib/cal/src</tt>. The two system actors are combined in a netlist file named <tt>switchled.nl</tt> that you can find into cal_demo's directory. The purpose of this demo is to read the state of the switches and button residing on the FPG-EYE and produce it switching on/off the appropriate leds on the board itself.
Open the Lattice Mico32 System and press the C/C++ button on the status bar: [[File:eclipse_empty_screen.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the C/C++ button that must be pressed]]
Let's create a standard C project: [[File:eclipse-standard-make-project.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the button which must be pressed to create a standard C project]]
Give the project a name you like (i.e. cal_demo) and beware not to use the default location suggested by the program but the directory where resides the cal_demo into the Erika's trunk: [[File:cal-demo-project-settings.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows how to properly edit the project settings for the cal_demo project]] Press the Finish button and your project will be added to the list of C/C++ projects.
Here's how your newly created project appears: [[File:cal_demo_project_created.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the files you will find once created a new cal_demo project]] The files present at this stage of the project are: * main.c: main file project needed to initialize components of the FPG-EYE that will be used in the project. The user can place here it's own code. * switchled.nl: the netlist file listing the actors present in our CAL project; it's because of netlist files that actors will be automatically included in the building process. To better understand where the system actors were injected into ERIKA's repository and where newly created CAL actors have to be saved have a look [[CAL support on ERIKA Enterprise | here]] * conf.oil: configuration file, part of the OSEK/VDX standard, that is used for OS and application configuration. You will find here, as application sources, both main.c and switchled.nl files. For further explanation about oil files please have a look at [[Tutorial: RT-Druid and OIL basics]] * makefile: makefile of our project * crt0ram.S: file that implements boot-code and exception handlers
To build the project right click on the cal_demo project and press the Build Project button: [[File:cal_demo_build_project.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows how to build the cal_demo project]]
The result of the compilation is shown in the next screenshot: [[File:cal_demo_compilation_successful.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the results of a correct building process]] As you can see in the previous screenshot there's a newly created folder named <tt>output/folder</tt> where object and dependency files are placed. Here you can find: * <tt>switchled.depend</tt> and <tt>switchled.xdf</tt>: these files are automatically created by the ACTORS makefiles in the process of creating the <tt>switchled.c</tt> from the netlist file present in our project * out.elf: the executable file
To clean the project right click on the cal_demo project and press the Clean Project button: [[File:cal_demo_clean_project.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows how to clean a project]]
== Create your second project: cal_demo_cal_actors ==
The main point of this second demo is that we used a CAL actor named <tt>gen.cal</tt>, a counter, instead of the previously used <tt>art_switch.c</tt> system actor; our counter is combined with the <tt>art_led.c</tt> system actor by the <tt>genled.nl</tt>. Both the netlist and the CAL actor files are placed in the project's directory. The purpose of this demo is to visualize the number produced by the counter switching on/off appropriately the leds placed into the FPG-EYE board
In order to create the project follow the steps described in the previous example, paying attention to the settings of the project:
[[File:cal_demo_cal_actors_project_settings.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows how to properly edit the project settings for the cal_demo_cal_actors project]]
Here's how your newly created project appears: [[File:cal_demo_cal_actors_project_created.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the files you will find once created a new cal_demo_cal_actors project]]
Looking at the files present at this stage and comparing them with the previous cal_demo example the main differences you will note are: * gen.cal: this is the CAL actor * genled.nl: this is the new netlist file. Please note the different nomenclature it to be used to address a system actor or a CAL one. To fully understand the meaning of the this nomenclature please refer to [[CAL support on ERIKA Enterprise]] * conf.oil: the application sources now present are main.c and genled.nl.
The result of a successful compilation (to be undertaken as explained in the previous example) is shown in the next screenshot: [[File:cal_demo_cal_actors_compilation_successful.png|center|thumb|200px|This screenshot shows the results of a correct building process of the cal_demo_cal_actors project]]
Looking at the newly created files you will notice some differences comparing with the previous example: * <tt>output/obj</tt>: there is now <tt>gen_0.c</tt> which is the C file created from the <tt>gen.cal</tt> CAL actor. In the process of obtaing <tt>gen_0.c</tt> and <tt>genled.c</tt> files the ACTORS makefiles created also <tt>gen_0.xlim</tt>, <tt>gen_0.par</tt> and <tt>art_led_0.par</tt> files that are stored into the project's directory.
== Create and compile a CAL project from scratch == You have now the basic knowledge to create your own CAL project from scratch. In the following you will find the steps to follow and the main points to be aware of: * create a directory for your project and copy into it the <tt>crt0ram.S</tt>, <tt>makefile</tt> <tt>conf.oil</tt> files. The latter will be opportunely modified in a secon moment. * create in the project's directory your <tt>main.c</tt> file and insert here your code * create CAL actors and/or system actors and a netlist file combining all the actors together. Please note that: ** CAL actors are created in CAL language and have to be placed in the project's directory. ** system actors have to be written in C language and placed in <tt>contrib/cal/src</tt> directory as explained in [[CAL support on ERIKA Enterprise]]. * edit the <tt>conf.oil</tt> file in order to add as applications sources your main C file and your netlist. Moreover pay attention to link correctly your platform library according to where it is placed on your system. For further explanation about oil files please have a look at [[Tutorial: RT-Druid and OIL basics]]
Now build your CAL application following the previous examples.

First of all, you need RT-Druid code and you can get it from svn. Then you need an editor: clearly you can use your preferred one, but if you are going to use eclipse, here is few hint.
= Code structure = RT-Druid source code is organized in several Eclipse projects; most of them correspond to a feature or a plugin. These projects are organized in the repository categories: * '''Products''': contains projects related to the packaging of distributions of RT-Druid * '''Source''': clearly the code of RT-Druid ** '''Core''': the main part ** '''Analysis''': plugins related to the analysis of a system described in RT-Druid ** '''Oil''': oil support * '''Testing''': all plugins related to the test of RT-Druid code
= Setting up eclipse = What you need to develop RT-Druid plugins is * '''java sdk''': i.e. the compiler. we suggest to use the oracle jdk 1.6 ([http://www.oracle.com/technetwork/java/javase/downloads/index.html here is the Java SE download page]) * '''Eclipse sdk''': if you do not have preferences or something already installed, take the ([http://www.eclipse.org/downloads/packages/eclipse-classic-37/indigor "classic" package of Eclipse]). Then you need to add few plugins, if you do not already have them: ** '''Emf''': emf update site is ([http://download.eclipse.org/modeling/emf/updates/releases/ here]). Suggested selection is Emf.sdk (it contains the code and more than what you need, but it is the fastest way) ** '''Gef''': gef update site is ([http://download.eclipse.org/tools/gef/updates/releases/ here]). Again we suggest the sdk pack: gef.sdk ** '''CDT''': cdt update site is ([http://download.eclipse.org/tools/cdt/releases/indigo/ here]). ALso here we suggest the sdk pack.
Even if they are not required, you can install also plugins for versioning like ([http://www.eclipse.org/subversive/downloads.php subversive]), or for bug reporting like ([http://www.eclipse.org/mylyn/downloads/ mylyn])
* '''Note''': you can find ([http://help.eclipse.org/indigo/topic/org.eclipse.platform.doc.user/tasks/tasks-34.htm here]) few instruction about how install plugins using eclise update manager
= Setting ant and output paths = In order to easily move RT-Druid plugins through various versions and installations of Eclipse, we use two variables ANT_HOME and MEM_OUTPUT_LOCATION. We can set both using the Eclipse preference window, opened through the '''Preferences''' command in the '''Window''' menu [[File:rtd_prefs.png]]
* '''ANT_HOME''' points to the ant plugin in the current installation of eclipse [[File:rtd_ant_home.png]]
* '''MEM_OUTPUT_LOCATION''' is the place where store binary files generated during Eclipse build. (Note that this path is not used by website and other production plugins). This allow to separate the source from the binary, with some useful effects like: ** it is possible to put outputs in a ram-disk ** compile the same code files with more than one version/instance of eclipse at the same time ** maintain clean the source code directories [[File:rtd_mem_output.png]]
= Importing projects = To import RT-Druid projects into your eclipse workspace, you have to select '''Import...''' from '''File menu''' [[File:rtd_import_01.png]]
Then select "Existing projects into workspace" [[File:rtd_import_02.png]]
The window requires the path on your filesystem where find RT-Druid source projects (in this example, the path is '''E:\work\RT-Druid'''). If the path is correct you should see the list of RT-Druid projects and you can select which import in your workspace. '''Copy project''' flag allows you to copy all files in your workspace, otherwise Eclipse will read and write directly in the path you give. Working set is useful to quickly select a group of projects. [[File:rtd_import_03.png]]
If you set ant and output paths, and if you have autobuild enabled (true by default) you should see Eclipse that start to compile all RT-Druid projects. [[File:rtd_import_04.png]]

== Setting ant and output paths == In order to easily move RT-Druid plugins through various versions and installations of Eclipse, we use two variables ANT_HOME and MEM_OUTPUT_LOCATION. We can set both using the Eclipse preference window, opened through the '''Preferences''' command in the '''Window''' menu
[[File:rtd_prefs.png|center|thumb|200px|Preferences location in the Eclipse menu]]
* '''ANT_HOME''' points to the ant plugin in the current installation of eclipse [[File:rtd_ant_home.png|center|thumb|300px|An example of ANT_HOME variable]]
* '''MEM_OUTPUT_LOCATION''' is the place where store binary files generated during Eclipse build. (Note that this path is not used by website and other production plugins). = Introduction = Before execute this simple tutorial follow installation procedure described in [[Tutorial:_Installing_scicoslab_and_generating_code_from_a_Scicos_diagram#Scicoslab_4.4.1_and_ScicosLab_Pack_10.0:_code_generator_for_FLEX_-_Installation_procedure | installig scicoslab tutorial]]
= Your first Scicos application for Easylab =
To create the easyest demo for easylab board follow the steps described in [[Tutorial:_Installing_scicoslab_and_generating_code_from_a_Scicos_diagram#Your_first_Scicos_application Your first Scicos Application for FLEX]] just make sure to use blocks from Easylab palette instead of the ones from FLEX palette.
This Chapter will guide you to the creation, compilation and execution of a first simple Scicos example on a FLEX Demo board. The example created in this tutorial can be found in the directory scicos_ee/examples/easylab_flex/Led_sin. inside scicos pack base directory. If you are looking for a prebuilt example, go directly to the next Section.

revision.text:
= Introduction =
This small tutorial describes the steps needed to integrate CAL language on Erika Enterprise for the Lattice Mico32 platform.
This tutorial has been tested on a board produced by Evidence. Moreover, the needed software has been installed and tested on an Ubuntu 10.10 maverick but the installation process should be adapted to almost all other releases.
Even if all the steps needed to run an application will be depicted, a preliminary knowledge on the Microchip MPLAB X IDE and its debug environment should be useful to the reader.

= Introduction =
This small tutorial describes the steps needed to integrate CAL language on Erika Enterprise for the Lattice Mico32 platform.
This tutorial has been tested on a board produced by Evidence. Moreover, the needed software has been installed and tested on an Ubuntu 10.10 maverick but the installation process should be adapted to almost all other releases.
Even if all the steps needed to run an application will be depicted, a preliminary knowledge on the Microchip MPLAB X IDE and its debug environment should be useful to the reader.

Even if all the steps needed to run an application will be depicted, a preliminary knowledge on the Microchip MPLAB X IDE and its debug environment should be useful to the reader.
= Note for Linux Users =
If you are using a Linux distribution please look carefully at the following warnings:
# The Evidence package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces. e.g. use <tt>~/Evidence</tt>. # The Scilab package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces: e.g. use <tt>~/Evidence/scicoslab-4.4b7</tt>. # It is strongly encouraged to adopt real paths instead of using symbolic links and aliases. # Please install all the Microchip compilers into their default directory (<tt>/opt/XXXX</tt>).

To update all the packages open a Terminal window and execute the following commands: 
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get upgrade
Now you have to install all the packages needed by the cal software to transform cal files in c files. So type: 
sudo apt-get install subversion 
sudo apt-get install java-common sun-java6-bin sun-java6-jre sun-java6-jdk sun-java6-source

For the purpose it has been used a virtual machine created with VMWare but all the test processes can be smoothly deployed on a phisical linux partition. Even if all the steps needed to run an application will be depicted, a preliminary knowledge on the actor's project and cal language would be useful to the reader. = Note for Linux Users = If you are using a Linux distribution please look carefully at the following warnings: # The Evidence package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces. e.g. use ~/Evidence. # The actorsproject package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces: e.g. use ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. # It is strongly encouraged to adopt real paths instead of using symbolic links and aliases. # Please install all the Lattice compilers into their default directory (/opt/XXXX). = Prerequisites = As the first step create a virtual machine with Ubuntu 10.10 as guest operating system. In our example we've used VMware Player 3.1.3 and installed WMware tools for linux version 8.4.5 version. After creating the virtual machine, before proceeding with the installation process, it would be useful to completely update the packages installed in your system to the latest version. To update all the packages open a Terminal window and execute the following commands: 
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get upgrade
Now install all the packages needed by the cal software to transform cal files in c files. So type: 
sudo apt-get install java-common sun-java6-bin sun-java6-jre sun-java6-jdk sun-java6-source
sudo apt-get install ant subversion csh libxml2-dev libsdl1.2-dev libgtk2.0-dev
= Downloading actor's project source code = You are now ready to download the actor's project on your system on a folder created for this purpose (i.e. ~/opendf): 
mkdir opendf
cd opendf
svn co https://opendf.svn.sourceforge.net/svnroot/opendf/trunk
Under the opendf's project trunk you will find all the actor's project source code needed for our purpose: ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject = Installing ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux = In order to install ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux follow the procedure described here:
http://erika.tuxfamily.org/wiki/index.php?title=Tutorial:_Installing_ERIKA_and_RT-Druid_on_a_Linux_host
For our tests we've used the eclipse_3_6_ready_to_use_LINUX_201101111314 version and installed it, under the ~/Evidence folder = Installing LatticeMico32 System on Linux = In order to install Lattice Semiconductor Corporation's LatticeMico32 System look in the following website:
http://www.latticesemi.com/
for the version that suites you the best. In the follow we will assume you will be using the same version as the one we've used, the 8.0.00.63 for Linux. Download the appropriate tar archive and put it on your hard disk, let's say in ~temp_lattice. After having created in your home the Lattice folder follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~temp_lattice
tar xf RL8.0.00.63.43.09_linux_lm32.tar
cd ../Lattice
../temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32/mico32_install.csh /home/user/temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32
Accept all the terms and agreements you will be prompted. When asked, tell the setup to install both gtool and mico32

http://erika.tuxfamily.org/wiki/index.php?title=Tutorial:_Installing_ERIKA_and_RT-Druid_on_a_Linux_host For our tests we've used the eclipse_3_6_ready_to_use_LINUX_201101111314 version and installed it, under the ~/Evidence folder = Installing LatticeMico32 System and ispVM System on Linux = In order to install Lattice Semiconductor Corporation's LatticeMico32 System look in the following website:
http://www.latticesemi.com/
for the version that suites you the best. In the follow we will assume you will be using the same version as the one we've used, the 8.0.00.63 for Linux. Download the appropriate tar archive and put it on your hard disk, let's say in ~temp_lattice. After having created in your home the ~/Lattice folder follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_lattice
tar xf RL8.0.00.63.43.09_linux_lm32.tar
cd ../Lattice/
../temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32/mico32_install.csh /home/user/temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32
rm -R ~/temp_lattice
Accept all the terms and agreements you will be prompted. When asked, tell the setup to install both gtool and Lattice Mico32 system Tools; moreover tell the setup you are not installing neither from a dvd drive, nor from a cd one. Next let's install ispVM System on our virtual machine. To do so download the ispVM System from the Lattice's website, for our tests we've used the 17.6 version for linux. Put the ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz file on a newly ~/temp_ispvm directory, create the ~/Lattice/ispvm folder and follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_ispvm
tar -xvzf ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz 
mv isptools/ ../Lattice/ispvm/
cd ~ && rm -R ~/temp_ispvm
Before launching for the first time the LatticeMico32 System we have to create and export some environment variables. Open up the ~/.profile file with a text editor (i.e. Gedit) and append the following lines: 
export ISPVM_DIR=~/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=~/Evidence/eclipse
Open a new Terminal window and export the newly created environment variables: 
export ISPVM_DIR=~/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=~/Evidence/eclipse
Now move to the directory where LatticeMico32 System resides and launch the executable file: 
cd ~/Lattice/LatticeMicoSystem/micosystem
./LatticeMico32Launcher

= Introduction = This small tutorial describes the steps needed to integrate CAL language in Erika Enterprise using a Lattice Mico32 platform. This tutorial has been tested on a board produced by Evidence in which we've integrated an FPGA using a Mico32 processor. The needed software has been installed and tested on Ubuntu 10.10 maverick but the installation process should be adapted to almost all other releases. For the purpose it has been used a virtual machine created with VMWare but all the test processes can be smoothly deployed on a physical linux machine. = Note for Linux Users = If you are using a Linux distribution please look carefully at the following warnings: # The Evidence package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces. e.g. use ~/Evidence. # The actorsproject package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces: e.g. use ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. # It is strongly encouraged to adopt real paths instead of using symbolic links and aliases. # Please install all the Lattice compilers into their default directory (/opt/XXXX). = Prerequisites = As the first step create a virtual machine with Ubuntu 10.10 as guest operating system. In our example we've used VMware Player 3.1.3 and installed WMware tools for linux version 8.4.5 version. After creating the virtual machine, before proceeding with the installation process, it would be useful to completely update the packages installed in your system to the latest version. To update all the packages open a Terminal window and execute the following commands: 
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get upgrade
Now install all the packages needed by the cal software to transform cal files in c files. So type: 
sudo apt-get install java-common sun-java6-bin sun-java6-jre sun-java6-jdk sun-java6-source
sudo apt-get install ant subversion csh libxml2-dev libsdl1.2-dev libgtk2.0-dev
= Downloading actor's project source code = You are now ready to download the actor's project on your system on a folder created for this purpose (i.e. ~/opendf): 
mkdir opendf
cd opendf
svn co https://opendf.svn.sourceforge.net/svnroot/opendf/trunk
Under the opendf's project trunk you will find all the actor's project source code needed for our purpose: ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject = Installing ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux = In order to install ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux follow the procedure described here:
http://erika.tuxfamily.org/wiki/index.php?title=Tutorial:_Installing_ERIKA_and_RT-Druid_on_a_Linux_host For our tests we've used the eclipse_3_6_ready_to_use_LINUX_201101111314 version and installed it, under the ~/Evidence folder = Installing LatticeMico32 System and ispVM System on Linux = In order to install Lattice Semiconductor Corporation's LatticeMico32 System look in the following website:
http://www.latticesemi.com/
for the version that suites you the best. In the follow we will assume you will be using the same version as the one we've used, the 8.0.00.63 for Linux. Download the appropriate tar archive and put it on your hard disk, let's say in ~temp_lattice. After having created in your home the ~/Lattice folder follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_lattice
tar xf RL8.0.00.63.43.09_linux_lm32.tar
cd ../Lattice/
../temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32/mico32_install.csh /home/user/temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32
rm -R ~/temp_lattice
Accept all the terms and agreements you will be prompted. When asked, tell the setup to install both gtool and Lattice Mico32 system Tools; moreover tell the setup you are not installing neither from a dvd drive, nor from a cd one. Next let's install ispVM System on our virtual machine. To do so download the ispVM System from the Lattice's website, for our tests we've used the 17.6 version for linux. Put the ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz file on a newly ~/temp_ispvm directory, create the ~/Lattice/ispvm folder and follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_ispvm
tar -xvzf ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz 
mv isptools/ ../Lattice/ispvm/
cd ~ && rm -R ~/temp_ispvm
= Downloading Erika's trunk = Let's proceed downloading the Erika's trunk where you will find the cal language libraries adapted to work in Erika Enterprise, system actors created in C language and a couple of demos which are the main focus of this tutorial. Create an appropriate folder, for instance ~/Evidence/Erika and type: 
cd ~/Evidence/Erika
svn co svn+ssh://user81@svn.tuxfamily.org/svnroot/erika/erikae/repos/ee/trunk/ee
= Export needed environment variables = Before launching for the first time the LatticeMico32 System we have to create and export some environment variables needed to compile projects into LatticeMico32 System. Open up the ~/.profile file with a text editor (i.e. Gedit) and append the following lines: 
export ISPVM_DIR=~/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=~/Evidence/eclipse
Open a new Terminal window and export the newly created environment variables: 
export ISPVM_DIR=~/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=~/Evidence/eclipse
Now move to the directory where LatticeMico32 System resides and launch the executable file: 
cd ~/Lattice/LatticeMicoSystem/micosystem
./LatticeMico32Launcher

Put the ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz file on a newly ~/temp_ispvm directory, create the ~/Lattice/ispvm folder and follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_ispvm
tar -xvzf ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz 
mv isptools/ ../Lattice/ispvm/
cd ~ && rm -R ~/temp_ispvm
= Downloading Erika's trunk = Let's proceed downloading the Erika's trunk where you will find the cal language libraries adapted to work in Erika Enterprise, system actors created in C language and a couple of demos which are the main focus of this tutorial. Create an appropriate folder, for instance ~/Evidence/Erika and type: 
cd ~/Evidence/Erika
svn co svn+ssh://user81@svn.tuxfamily.org/svnroot/erika/erikae/repos/ee/trunk/ee
= Export needed environment variables = Before launching for the first time the LatticeMico32 System we have to create and export some environment variables needed to compile projects into LatticeMico32 System. Open up the ~/.profile file with a text editor (i.e. Gedit) and append the following lines: 
export ISPVM_DIR=~/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=~/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=~/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Open a new Terminal window and export the newly created environment variables: 
export ISPVM_DIR=~/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=~/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=~/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
= Launch LatticeMico32 System = Once exported all the needed environment variables you are ready to launch the environment. Move to the directory where LatticeMico32 System resides and launch the executable file: 
cd ~/Lattice/micosystem
./LatticeMico32Launcher

= Introduction = This small tutorial describes the steps needed to integrate CAL language in Erika Enterprise using a Lattice Mico32 platform. This tutorial has been tested on a board produced by Evidence in which we've integrated an FPGA using a Mico32 processor. The needed software has been installed and tested on Ubuntu 10.10 maverick but the installation process should be adapted to almost all other releases. For the purpose it has been used a virtual machine created with VMWare but all the test processes can be smoothly deployed on a physical linux machine. = Note for Linux Users = If you are using a Linux distribution please look carefully at the following warnings: # The Evidence package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces. e.g. use ~/Evidence. # The actorsproject package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces: e.g. use ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. # It is strongly encouraged to adopt real paths instead of using symbolic links and aliases. # Please install all the Lattice compilers into their default directory (/opt/XXXX). = Prerequisites = In order to download the Erika's source code create an account in
http://http://erika.tuxfamily.org/ Let's assume you've created an account with username: user Create then a virtual machine with Ubuntu 10.10 maverick as guest operating system. In our example we've used VMware Player 3.1.3 and installed WMware tools for linux version 8.4.5 version. All the tests can be smoothly deployed on a Ubuntu 10.10 physical machine. After creating the virtual machine, before proceeding with the installation process, it would be useful to completely update the packages installed in your system to the latest version. To update all the packages open a Terminal window and execute the following commands: 
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get upgrade

sudo apt-get install java-common sun-java6-bin sun-java6-jre sun-java6-jdk sun-java6-source
sudo apt-get install ant subversion csh libxml2-dev libsdl1.2-dev libgtk2.0-dev
= Downloading actor's project source code = You are now ready to download the actor's project on your system on a folder created for this purpose (i.e. ~/opendf): 
mkdir opendf
cd opendf
svn co https://opendf.svn.sourceforge.net/svnroot/opendf/trunk
Under the opendf's project trunk you will find all the actor's project source code needed for our purpose: ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. Move to this directory and install the tools provided by the actor's project by writing in a Terminal window: 
make
make install

for the version that suites you the best. In the follow we will assume you will be using the same version as the one we've used, the 8.0.00.63 for Linux. ../temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32/mico32_install.csh /home/user/temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32
rm -R ~/temp_lattice

Under the opendf's project trunk you will find all the actor's project source code needed for our purpose: ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. Move to this directory and install the tools provided by the actor's project by writing in a Terminal window: 
make
make install
Now you will have all the tools needed to convert cal files into c files (xlim2c compiler and others) under the directory:~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject/lib = Installing ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux = In order to install ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux follow the procedure described here:
http://erika.tuxfamily.org/wiki/index.php?title=Tutorial:_Installing_ERIKA_and_RT-Druid_on_a_Linux_host For our tests we've used the eclipse_3_6_ready_to_use_LINUX_201101111314 version and installed it, under the ~/Evidence folder = Installing LatticeMico32 System and ispVM System on Linux = In order to install Lattice Semiconductor Corporation's LatticeMico32 System look in the following website:
http://www.latticesemi.com/
for the version that suites you the best. In the follow we will assume you will be using the same version as the one we've used, the 8.0.00.63 for Linux. Download the appropriate tar archive and put it on your hard disk, let's say in ~temp_lattice. After having created in your home the ~/Lattice folder follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_lattice
tar xf RL8.0.00.63.43.09_linux_lm32.tar
cd ../Lattice/
../temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32/mico32_install.csh /home/user/temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32
rm -R ~/temp_lattice
Accept all the terms and agreements you will be prompted. When asked, tell the setup to install both gtool and Lattice Mico32 system Tools; moreover tell the setup you are not installing neither from a dvd drive, nor from a cd one. Next let's install ispVM System on our virtual machine. To do so download the ispVM System from the Lattice's website, for our tests we've used the 17.6 version for linux. Put the ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz file on a newly ~/temp_ispvm directory, create the ~/Lattice/ispvm folder and follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_ispvm
tar -xvzf ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz 
mv isptools/ ../Lattice/ispvm/
cd ~ && rm -R ~/temp_ispvm
= Downloading Erika's trunk = Let's proceed downloading the Erika's trunk where you will find the cal language libraries adapted to work in Erika Enterprise, system actors created in C language and a couple of demos which are the main focus of this tutorial. Create an appropriate folder, for instance ~/Evidence/Erika and type: 
cd ~/Evidence/Erika
svn co svn+ssh://user81@svn.tuxfamily.org/svnroot/erika/erikae/repos/ee/trunk/ee
= Export needed environment variables = Before launching for the first time the LatticeMico32 System we have to create and export some environment variables needed to compile projects into LatticeMico32 System. Open up the ~/.profile file with a text editor (i.e. Gedit) and append the following lines: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Open a new Terminal window and export the newly created environment variables: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Or, if you prefer, reboot your system. = Launch LatticeMico32 System = Employing the same Terminal window used previously to export the needed environment variables move to the directory where LatticeMico32 System resides and launch the executable file: 
cd ~/Lattice/micosystem
./LatticeMico32Launcher

= Introduction = This tutorial describes the steps needed to integrate CAL language into Erika Enterprise in order to create projects to be compiled in a Lattice Mico32 platform. = Introduction = This tutorial describes the steps needed to integrate the CAL language into Erika Enterprise in order to create projects to be compiled and run in a Lattice Mico32 platform. The tutorial has been tested on a board produced by Evidence in which we've integrated an FPGA using a Mico32 processor. The needed software has been installed and tested on a virtual machine running Ubuntu 10.10 maverick but the installation process could be adapted to almost all other releases. The tests can moreover be smoothly deployed on a physical Linux machine. = Note for Linux Users = Since it has to be used a Linux distribution please look carefully at the following warnings: # The Evidence package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces. e.g. use ~/Evidence. # The actorsproject package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces: e.g. use ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. # It is strongly encouraged to adopt real paths instead of using symbolic links and aliases. # Please install all the Lattice compilers into their default directory (/opt/XXXX). = Prerequisites = In order to download the Erika's source code create an account in
http://http://erika.tuxfamily.org/ Let's assume you've created an account with username: user Create then a virtual machine with Ubuntu 10.10 maverick as guest operating system. In our example we've used VMware Player 3.1.3 and installed WMware tools for linux version 8.4.5 version. All the tests can be smoothly deployed on a Ubuntu 10.10 physical machine. After creating the virtual machine, before proceeding with the installation process, it would be useful to completely update the packages installed in your system to the latest version. To update all the packages open a Terminal window and execute the following commands: 
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get upgrade
Now install all the packages needed by the cal software to transform cal files in c files. So type: 
sudo apt-get install java-common sun-java6-bin sun-java6-jre sun-java6-jdk sun-java6-source
sudo apt-get install ant subversion csh gawk libxml2-dev libsdl1.2-dev libgtk2.0-dev
= Downloading actor's project source code = You are now ready to download the actor's project on your system on a folder created for this purpose (i.e. ~/opendf): 
mkdir opendf
cd opendf
svn co https://opendf.svn.sourceforge.net/svnroot/opendf/trunk
Under the opendf's project trunk you will find all the actor's project source code needed for our purpose: ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. Move to this directory and install the tools provided by the actor's project by writing in a Terminal window: 
make
make install
Now you will have all the tools needed to convert cal files into c files (xlim2c compiler and others) under the directory:~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject/lib = Installing ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux = In order to install ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux follow the procedure described here:
http://erika.tuxfamily.org/wiki/index.php?title=Tutorial:_Installing_ERIKA_and_RT-Druid_on_a_Linux_host For our tests we've used the eclipse_3_6_ready_to_use_LINUX_201101111314 version and installed it, under the ~/Evidence folder = Installing LatticeMico32 System and ispVM System on Linux = In order to install Lattice Semiconductor Corporation's LatticeMico32 System look in the following website:
http://www.latticesemi.com/
for the version that suites you the best. In the follow we will assume you will be using the same version as the one we've used, the 8.0.00.63 for Linux. Download the appropriate tar archive and put it on your hard disk, let's say in ~temp_lattice. After having created in your home the ~/Lattice folder follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_lattice
tar xf RL8.0.00.63.43.09_linux_lm32.tar
cd ../Lattice/
../temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32/mico32_install.csh /home/user/temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32
rm -R ~/temp_lattice
Accept all the terms and agreements you will be prompted. When asked, tell the setup to install both gtool and Lattice Mico32 system Tools; moreover tell the setup you are not installing neither from a dvd drive, nor from a cd one. Next let's install ispVM System on our virtual machine. To do so download the ispVM System from the Lattice's website, for our tests we've used the 17.6 version for linux. Put the ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz file on a newly ~/temp_ispvm directory, create the ~/Lattice/ispvm folder and follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_ispvm
tar -xvzf ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz 
mv isptools/ ../Lattice/ispvm/
cd ~ && rm -R ~/temp_ispvm
= Downloading Erika's trunk = Let's proceed downloading the Erika's trunk where you will find the cal language libraries adapted to work in Erika Enterprise, system actors created in C language and a couple of demos which are the main focus of this tutorial. Create an appropriate folder, for instance ~/Evidence/Erika and type: 
cd ~/Evidence/Erika
svn co svn+ssh://user81@svn.tuxfamily.org/svnroot/erika/erikae/repos/ee/trunk/ee
= Export needed environment variables = Before launching for the first time the LatticeMico32 System we have to create and export some environment variables needed to compile projects into LatticeMico32 System. export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Open a new Terminal window and export the newly created environment variables: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Or, if you prefer, reboot your system. = Launch LatticeMico32 System = Employing the same Terminal window used previously to export the needed environment variables move to the directory where LatticeMico32 System resides and launch the executable file: 
cd ~/Lattice/micosystem
./LatticeMico32Launcher

Download the appropriate tar archive and put it on your hard disk, let's say in ~temp_lattice. After having created in your home the ~/Lattice folder follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_lattice
tar xf RL8.0.00.63.43.09_linux_lm32.tar
cd ../Lattice/
../temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32/mico32_install.csh /home/user/temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32
rm -R ~/temp_lattice
Accept all the terms and agreements you will be prompted. When asked, tell the setup to install both gtool and Lattice Mico32 system Tools; moreover tell the setup you are not installing neither from a dvd drive, nor from a cd one. Next let's install ispVM System on our virtual machine. To do so download the ispVM System from the Lattice's website, for our tests we've used the 17.6 version for linux. Put the ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz file on a newly ~/temp_ispvm directory, create the ~/Lattice/ispvm folder and follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_ispvm
tar -xvzf ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz 
mv isptools/ ../Lattice/ispvm/
cd ~ && rm -R ~/temp_ispvm
= Downloading Erika's trunk = Let's proceed downloading the Erika's trunk where you will find the cal language libraries adapted to work in Erika Enterprise, system actors created in C language and a couple of demos which are the main focus of this tutorial. Create an appropriate folder, for instance ~/Evidence/Erika and type: 
cd ~/Evidence/Erika
svn co svn+ssh://user81@svn.tuxfamily.org/svnroot/erika/erikae/repos/ee/trunk/ee
= Export needed environment variables = Before launching for the first time the LatticeMico32 System we have to create and export some environment variables needed to compile projects into LatticeMico32 System. Open up the ~/.profile file with a text editor (i.e. Gedit) and append the following lines: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Open a new Terminal window and export the newly created environment variables: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Or, if you prefer, reboot your system. = Launch LatticeMico32 System = Employing the same Terminal window used previously to export the needed environment variables move to the directory where LatticeMico32 System resides and launch the executable file: 
cd ~/Lattice/micosystem
./LatticeMico32Launcher

= Introduction = This tutorial describes the steps needed to integrate the CAL language into Erika Enterprise in order to create projects to be compiled and run in a Lattice Mico32 platform. The tutorial has been tested on a board produced by Evidence in which we've integrated an FPGA using a Mico32 processor. The needed software has been installed and tested on a virtual machine running Ubuntu 10.10 maverick but the installation process could be adapted to almost all other releases. The tests can moreover be smoothly deployed on a physical Linux machine. = Note for Linux Users = Since it has to be used a Linux distribution please look carefully at the following warnings: # The Evidence package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces. e.g. use ~/Evidence. # The actorsproject package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces: e.g. use ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. # It is strongly encouraged to adopt real paths instead of using symbolic links and aliases. # Please install all the actor's project compilers into their default directory, for instance ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject/bin if the actor's project is located in ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject = Prerequisites = In order to download the Erika's source code create an account in
http://http://erika.tuxfamily.org/ In the future we will assume you've created an account with username: erikauser Create then a virtual machine with Ubuntu 10.10 maverick as guest operating system. In our example we've used VMware Player 3.1.3 and installed WMware tools for linux version 8.4.5 version. All the tests can be smoothly deployed on a Ubuntu 10.10 physical machine. After creating the virtual machine, before proceeding with the installation process, it would be useful to completely update the packages installed in your system to the latest version. To update all the packages open a Terminal window and execute the following commands: 
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get upgrade
Now install all the packages needed by the cal software to transform cal files in c files. So type: 
sudo apt-get install java-common sun-java6-bin sun-java6-jre sun-java6-jdk sun-java6-source
sudo apt-get install ant subversion csh gawk libxml2-dev libsdl1.2-dev libgtk2.0-dev
= Downloading actor's project source code = You are now ready to download the actor's project on your system on a folder created for this purpose (i.e. ~/opendf): 
mkdir opendf
cd opendf
svn co https://opendf.svn.sourceforge.net/svnroot/opendf/trunk
Under the opendf's project trunk you will find all the actor's project source code needed for our purpose: ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. Move to this directory and install the tools provided by the actor's project by writing in a Terminal window: 
make
make install

The tests can moreover be smoothly deployed on a physical Linux machine. = Note for Linux Users = Since it has to be used a Linux distribution please look carefully at the following warnings: # The Evidence package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces. e.g. use ~/Evidence. # The actorsproject package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces: e.g. use ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. # It is strongly encouraged to adopt real paths instead of using symbolic links and aliases. # Please install all the actor's project compilers into their default directory, for instance ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject/bin if the actor's project is located in ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject = Prerequisites = In order to download the Erika's source code create an account in
http://http://erika.tuxfamily.org/ In the future we will assume you've created an account with username: erikauser Create then a virtual machine with Ubuntu 10.10 maverick as guest operating system. In our example we've used VMware Player 3.1.3 and installed WMware tools for linux version 8.4.5 version. Anyway all the tests can be smoothly deployed on a Linux physical machine. After creating the virtual machine, before proceeding with the installation process, it would be useful to completely update the packages installed in your system to the latest version. To update all the packages open a Terminal window and execute the following commands: 
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get upgrade
Now install all the packages needed to compile our projects. Type: 
sudo apt-get install java-common sun-java6-bin sun-java6-jre sun-java6-jdk sun-java6-source
sudo apt-get install ant subversion csh gawk libxml2-dev libsdl1.2-dev libgtk2.0-dev
= Downloading actor's project source code = You are now ready to download the actor's project on your system on a folder created for this purpose (i.e. ~/opendf): 
mkdir opendf
cd opendf
svn co https://opendf.svn.sourceforge.net/svnroot/opendf/trunk
Under the opendf's project trunk you will find all the actor's project source code needed for our purpose: ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. Move to this directory and install the tools provided by the actor's project by writing in a Terminal window: 
make
make install
Now you have all the tools needed to convert cal files into c files (xlim2c compiler and others) under the directory:~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject/lib = Installing ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux = In order to install ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux follow the procedure described here:
http://erika.tuxfamily.org/wiki/index.php?title=Tutorial:_Installing_ERIKA_and_RT-Druid_on_a_Linux_host For our tests we've used the eclipse_3_6_ready_to_use_LINUX_201101111314 version and installed it, under the ~/Evidence folder = Installing LatticeMico32 System and ispVM System on Linux = In order to install Lattice Semiconductor Corporation's LatticeMico32 System look in the following website:
http://www.latticesemi.com/
for the version that suites you the best. In the follow we will assume you will be using the same version as the one we've used, the 8.0.00.63 for Linux. Download the appropriate tar archive and put it on your hard disk, let's say in ~temp_lattice. After having created in your home the ~/Lattice folder follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_lattice
tar xf RL8.0.00.63.43.09_linux_lm32.tar
cd ../Lattice/
../temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32/mico32_install.csh /home/user/temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32
rm -R ~/temp_lattice
Accept all the terms and agreements you will be prompted. When asked, tell the setup to install both gtool and Lattice Mico32 system Tools; moreover tell the setup you are not installing neither from a dvd drive, nor from a cd one. Next let's install ispVM System on our virtual machine. To do so download the ispVM System from the Lattice's website, for our tests we've used the 17.6 version for linux. Put the ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz file on a newly ~/temp_ispvm directory, create the ~/Lattice/ispvm folder and follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_ispvm
tar -xvzf ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz 
mv isptools/ ../Lattice/ispvm/
cd ~ && rm -R ~/temp_ispvm
= Downloading Erika's trunk = Let's proceed downloading the Erika's trunk where you will find the cal language libraries adapted to work in Erika Enterprise, system actors created in C language and a couple of demos which are the main focus of this tutorial. Create an appropriate folder, for instance ~/Evidence/Erika and type: 
cd ~/Evidence/Erika
svn co svn+ssh://erikauser@svn.tuxfamily.org/svnroot/erika/erikae/repos/ee/trunk/ee
= Export needed environment variables = Before launching for the first time the LatticeMico32 System we have to create and export some environment variables needed to compile projects into LatticeMico32 System. Open up the ~/.profile file with a text editor (i.e. Gedit) and append the following lines: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Open a new Terminal window and export the newly created environment variables: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Or, if you prefer, reboot your system. = Launch LatticeMico32 System = Employing the same Terminal window used previously to export the needed environment variables move to the directory where LatticeMico32 System resides and launch the executable file: 
cd ~/Lattice/micosystem
./LatticeMico32Launcher

cd ~/temp_lattice
tar xf RL8.0.00.63.43.09_linux_lm32.tar
cd ../Lattice/
../temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32/mico32_install.csh /home/user/temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32
rm -R ~/temp_lattice
Accept all the terms and agreements you will be prompted. When asked, tell the setup to install both gtool and Lattice Mico32 system Tools; moreover tell the setup you are not installing neither from a dvd drive, nor from a cd one. Next let's install ispVM System on our virtual machine. To do so download the ispVM System from the Lattice's website, for our tests we've used the 17.6 version for linux. Put the ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz file on a newly ~/temp_ispvm directory, create the ~/Lattice/ispvm folder and follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_ispvm
tar -xvzf ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz 
mv isptools/ ../Lattice/ispvm/
cd ~ && rm -R ~/temp_ispvm
= Downloading Erika's trunk = Let's proceed downloading the Erika's trunk where you will find the cal language libraries adapted to work in Erika Enterprise, system actors created in C language and a couple of demos which are the main focus of this tutorial. Create an appropriate folder, for instance ~/Evidence/Erika and type: 
cd ~/Evidence/Erika
svn co svn+ssh://erikauser@svn.tuxfamily.org/svnroot/erika/erikae/repos/ee/trunk/ee
= Export needed environment variables = Before launching for the first time the LatticeMico32 System we have to create and export some environment variables needed to compile projects into LatticeMico32 System. Open up the ~/.profile file with a text editor (i.e. Gedit) and append the following lines: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Open a new Terminal window and export the newly created environment variables: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Or, if you prefer, reboot your system. = Launch LatticeMico32 System = Employing the same Terminal window used previously to export the needed environment variables move to the directory where LatticeMico32 System resides and launch the executable file: 
cd ~/Lattice/micosystem
./LatticeMico32Launcher

= Introduction = This tutorial describes the steps needed to integrate the CAL language into Erika Enterprise in order to create projects to be compiled and run in a Lattice Mico32 platform. The tutorial has been tested on a board produced by Evidence in which we've integrated an FPGA using a Mico32 processor. The needed software has been installed and tested on a virtual machine running Ubuntu 10.10 maverick but the installation process could be adapted to almost all other releases. The tests can moreover be smoothly deployed on a physical Linux machine. = Note for Linux Users = Since it has to be used a Linux distribution please look carefully at the following warnings: # The Evidence package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces. e.g. use ~/Evidence. # The actorsproject package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces: e.g. use ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. # It is strongly encouraged to adopt real paths instead of using symbolic links and aliases. # Please install all the actor's project compilers into their default directory, for instance ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject/bin if the actor's project is located in ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject = Prerequisites = In order to download the Erika's source code create an account in
http://http://erika.tuxfamily.org/ We will assume for our tutorial that you've created an account with username: erikauser Create then a virtual machine with Ubuntu 10.10 maverick as guest operating system. In our example we've used VMware Player 3.1.3 and installed WMware tools for linux version 8.4.5 version. Anyway all the tests can be smoothly deployed on a Linux physical machine. After creating the virtual machine, before proceeding with the installation process, it would be useful to completely update the packages installed in your system to the latest version. To update all the packages open a Terminal window and execute the following commands: 
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get upgrade
Now install all the packages needed to compile our projects. Type: 
sudo apt-get install java-common sun-java6-bin sun-java6-jre sun-java6-jdk sun-java6-source
sudo apt-get install ant subversion csh gawk libxml2-dev libsdl1.2-dev libgtk2.0-dev
= Downloading actor's project source code = You are now ready to download the actor's project on your system on a folder created for this purpose (i.e. ~/opendf): 
mkdir opendf
cd opendf
svn co https://opendf.svn.sourceforge.net/svnroot/opendf/trunk
Under the opendf's project trunk you will find all the actor's project source code needed for our purpose: ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. Move to this directory and install the tools provided by the actor's project by writing in a Terminal window: 
make
make install
Now you have all the tools needed to convert cal files into c files (xlim2c compiler and others) under the directory:~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject/bin = Installing ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux = In order to install ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux follow the procedure described here:
http://erika.tuxfamily.org/wiki/index.php?title=Tutorial:_Installing_ERIKA_and_RT-Druid_on_a_Linux_host For our tests we've used the eclipse_3_6_ready_to_use_LINUX_201101111314 version and installed it under the ~/Evidence folder so that you can find the eclipse directory under ~/Evidence/eclipse = Installing LatticeMico32 System and ispVM System on Linux = In order to install LatticeMico32 System look in the following website:

The tutorial has been tested on a board produced by Evidence in which we've integrated an FPGA using a Mico32 processor. The needed software has been installed and tested on a virtual machine running Ubuntu 10.10 maverick but the installation process could be adapted to almost all other releases. The tests can moreover be smoothly deployed on a physical Linux machine. = Note for Linux Users = Since it has to be used a Linux distribution please look carefully at the following warnings: # The Evidence package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces. e.g. use ~/Evidence. # The actorsproject package installation path should NOT contain directory name with spaces: e.g. use ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. # It is strongly encouraged to adopt real paths instead of using symbolic links and aliases. # Please install all the actor's project compilers into their default directory, for instance ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject/bin if the actor's project is located in ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject = Prerequisites = In order to download the Erika's source code create an account in
http://http://erika.tuxfamily.org/ We will assume for our tutorial that you've created an account with username: erikauser Create then a virtual machine with Ubuntu 10.10 maverick as guest operating system. In our example we've used VMware Player 3.1.3 and installed WMware tools for linux version 8.4.5 version. Anyway all the tests can be smoothly deployed on a Linux physical machine. After creating the virtual machine, before proceeding with the installation process, it would be useful to completely update the packages installed in your system to the latest version. To update all the packages open a Terminal window and execute the following commands: 
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get upgrade
Now install all the packages needed to compile our projects. Type: 
sudo apt-get install java-common sun-java6-bin sun-java6-jre sun-java6-jdk sun-java6-source
sudo apt-get install ant subversion csh gawk libxml2-dev libsdl1.2-dev libgtk2.0-dev
= Downloading actor's project source code = You are now ready to download the actor's project on your system on a folder created for this purpose (i.e. ~/opendf): 
mkdir opendf
cd opendf
svn co https://opendf.svn.sourceforge.net/svnroot/opendf/trunk
Under the opendf's project trunk you will find all the actor's project source code needed for our purpose: ~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject. Move to this directory and install the tools provided by the actor's project by writing in a Terminal window: 
make
make install
Now you have all the tools needed to convert cal files into c files (xlim2c compiler and others) under the directory:~/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject/bin = Installing ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux = In order to install ERIKA Enterprise and RT-Druid on Linux follow the procedure described here:
http://erika.tuxfamily.org/wiki/index.php?title=Tutorial:_Installing_ERIKA_and_RT-Druid_on_a_Linux_host For our tests we've used the eclipse_3_6_ready_to_use_LINUX_201101111314 version and installed it under the ~/Evidence folder so that you can find the eclipse directory under ~/Evidence/eclipse = Installing LatticeMico32 System and ispVM System on Linux = The LatticeMico32 System can be found at downloaded at the following website
http://www.latticesemi.com/; for our tutorial we've chosen the 8.0.00.63 version for Linux. Download the related tar archive and put it on your hard disk, for instance in ~/temp_lattice. After having created in your home the ~/Lattice folder follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_lattice
tar xf RL8.0.00.63.43.09_linux_lm32.tar
cd ../Lattice/
../temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32/mico32_install.csh /home/user/temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32
rm -R ~/temp_lattice
Accept all the terms and agreements you will be prompted. When asked, tell the setup to install both gtool and Lattice Mico32 system Tools; moreover tell the setup you are not installing neither from a dvd drive, nor from a cd one. Next let's install ispVM System on our virtual machine. To do so download the ispVM System from the Lattice's website, for our tests we've used the 17.6 version for linux. Put the ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz file on a newly ~/temp_ispvm directory, create the ~/Lattice/ispvm folder and follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_ispvm
tar -xvzf ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz 
mv isptools/ ../Lattice/ispvm/
cd ~ && rm -R ~/temp_ispvm
= Downloading Erika's trunk = Let's proceed downloading the Erika's trunk where you will find the cal language libraries adapted to work in Erika Enterprise, system actors created in C language and a couple of demos which are the main focus of this tutorial. Create an appropriate folder, for instance ~/Evidence/Erika and type: 
cd ~/Evidence/Erika
svn co svn+ssh://erikauser@svn.tuxfamily.org/svnroot/erika/erikae/repos/ee/trunk/ee
= Export needed environment variables = Before launching for the first time the LatticeMico32 System we have to create and export some environment variables needed to compile projects into LatticeMico32 System. Open up the ~/.profile file with a text editor (i.e. Gedit) and append the following lines: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Open a new Terminal window and export the newly created environment variables: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Or, if you prefer, reboot your system. = Launch LatticeMico32 System = Employing the same Terminal window used previously to export the needed environment variables move to the directory where LatticeMico32 System resides and launch the executable file: 
cd ~/Lattice/micosystem
./LatticeMico32Launcher

cd ../Lattice/
../temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32/mico32_install.csh /home/user/temp_lattice/RL8.0.00.63.43.09_lm32
rm -R ~/temp_lattice
Accept all the terms and agreements you will be prompted. When asked, tell the setup to install both gtool and Lattice Mico32 system Tools and point out you are not installing neither from a dvd drive, nor from a cd one. Next install ispVM System on our virtual machine. To do so download the ispVM System from the Lattice's website, for our tests we've used the 17.6 version for linux. Put the ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz file on a newly ~/temp_ispvm directory, create the ~/Lattice/ispvm folder and follow the steps reported below: 
cd ~/temp_ispvm
tar -xvzf ispvm_v17_6_linux.tar.gz 
mv isptools/ ../Lattice/ispvm/
cd ~ && rm -R ~/temp_ispvm
= Downloading Erika's trunk = Let's proceed downloading the Erika's trunk where you will find the cal language libraries adapted to work in Erika Enterprise, system actors created in C language and a couple of demos which are the main focus of this tutorial. Create an appropriate folder, for instance ~/Evidence/Erika and type: 
cd ~/Evidence/Erika
svn co svn+ssh://erikauser@svn.tuxfamily.org/svnroot/erika/erikae/repos/ee/trunk/ee
= Export needed environment variables = Before launching for the first time the LatticeMico32 System we have to create and export some environment variables needed to compile projects into LatticeMico32 System. Open up the ~/.profile file with a text editor (i.e. Gedit) and append the following lines: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Open a new Terminal window and export the newly created environment variables: 
export ISPVM_DIR=/home/user/Lattice/ispvm/isptools/ispvmsystem/
export RTDRUID_ECLIPSE_HOME=/home/user/Evidence/eclipse
export EEBASE=/home/user/Evidence/Erika/ee
export CAL_BASE=/home/user/opendf/trunk/contrib/actorsproject
export ACTORS_JAVA=/usr/bin/java
Or, if you prefer, reboot your system. = Launch LatticeMico32 System = Employing the same Terminal window used previously to export the needed environment variables move to the directory where LatticeMico32 System resides and launch the executable file: 
cd ~/Lattice/micosystem
./LatticeMico32Launcher
